patterns.name: AI imagery clichés
patterns.summary: Images about artificial intelligence fall back on a small set of stock motifs: white humanoid robots, a robot hand reaching for a human hand in the pose of The Creation of Adam, glowing or half-circuit brains, blue circuit boards and holographic panels, descending code, and an overabundance of blue. Research on AI stock imagery documents the set and its misleading effect; a small test found humanoids or robots in all 20 images an image model generated for the plain prompt "artificial intelligence", against 11 of the first 20 results of a stock library.

detector.rubric: First decide whether the image illustrates AI, machine learning, automation or a generic digital topic. If it does, flag it when its main motif is one of these: a humanoid or white robot, especially one thinking, writing or working at screens; a robot hand touching or reaching for a human hand; a brain that glows, is built from circuits or particles, or floats above a chip; descending or floating code; holographic interface panels; a dominant blue palette of nodes, networks and circuitry with no concrete application. Count one hit per image. Does not count: images of actual robots in actual use (an industrial arm on an assembly line, a delivery robot on a sidewalk); diagrams or screenshots of real systems; neuroscience images of real brains; images whose brief is a critique or parody of these clichés. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Header image for an article on AI in hospitals: a white humanoid robot touching a glowing blue holographic display, with no doctors or patients in sight.
A human hand and a robotic hand reaching toward each other against a blue background, fingertips almost touching with a spark of light between them.
A translucent brain made of glowing circuit lines floating above a microchip on a dark blue background.
negative: Photo of a radiologist reviewing a scan with the region flagged by detection software highlighted on the monitor.
Industrial robot arms welding car bodies in a factory hall.
Screenshot of a chatbot interface showing a real conversation.

patterns.legitimate_use: Real robots in real use, real interfaces, real people working with AI systems, and images that quote the clichés knowingly for critique or satire.
patterns.fix: Replace the motif with the concrete application and the people involved: the clinician and the software on the screen, the warehouse worker and the sorting system, the data center, the labelling work, the dataset. Take colors from the setting instead of default blue.
patterns.prevention: When illustrating an AI or technology topic, describe the specific application, place and people: who uses which system for what ("a pharmacist checks a dosage warning on a desktop screen in a small pharmacy"). Take the palette from that setting. Ask for humanoid robots, glowing brains, touching hands, floating code or holograms only when the story is about exactly those things.

sources.note: Elements to avoid: the colour blue, descending code, the human brain, science fiction references, white robots, white men in suits, anthropomorphism, variations on The Creation of Adam.
Excessive blue, androgyne faces, half-flesh half-circuit brains, Creation of Adam variations, code waving in space.
Stable Diffusion: 20 of 20 images for 'artificial intelligence' show humanoids or robots versus 11 of 20 stock results; 19 of 20 with domain prompts.

patterns.name: Anatomical errors
patterns.summary: Bodies that cannot exist: missing, extra or merged fingers, absent fingernails, implausible hand proportions, misaligned or non-circular pupils, glossy hollow eyes, teeth in odd numbers or fused with the lips, extra or missing limbs, joints bending the wrong way, body parts merging between people. Current models make these errors less often and more subtly, which is why a close look at hands, eyes and mouths still pays off.

detector.rubric: Inspect every visible hand, face and limb at full resolution. Flag the image if any person or animal shows an anatomical impossibility: a wrong number of fingers or toes, fused or branching fingers, missing nails, a thumb on the wrong side; pupils of different shapes or directions, irises bleeding into the white; too many or uneven teeth, teeth merging with lips or tongue; an extra, missing or detached limb; a joint bent beyond its range; body parts of two people merging; a neck or torso of impossible length. Count one hit per image regardless of how many errors it has. Does not count: hands or limbs hidden by objects or cropping in a plausible way; motion blur, low resolution or compression that hides detail; real conditions (a missing finger, a prosthesis) shown as such; stylized conventions such as four-fingered cartoon hands or caricature. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Photo-style image of a woman holding a coffee cup with six fingers on her right hand, two of them merged at the base.
Close-up of a smiling man whose front teeth are uneven in number and blend into his lower lip.
Image of a couple holding hands in which their fingers merge into one shared hand.
negative: Photo of a hand partly in a coat pocket, three fingers visible and plausibly placed.
Cartoon character with four-fingered gloved hands in a classic animation style.
Portrait of a person with a visible prosthetic arm that is part of the story.

patterns.legitimate_use: None for realistic images. Stylized conventions such as four-fingered cartoon hands and real anatomy such as prosthetics or limb differences are not errors.
patterns.fix: Regenerate or inpaint the affected region with a crop that shows the anatomy clearly; simplify the pose (a hand resting flat, holding one simple object); compare with a reference photo; if the region cannot be repaired, recrop so it leaves the frame.
patterns.prevention: Choose poses that keep anatomy readable. Describe what each hand does in concrete terms ("both hands resting flat on the table", "right hand holding a mug by its handle"), prefer separate figures to interlaced fingers and overlapping crowds when the story allows, and ask for a closed-mouth smile when teeth add nothing. Review hands, eyes and teeth at full size before using the image.

sources.note: Missing, extra and merged fingers, nonexistent fingernails; misaligned or non-circular pupils; teeth overlapping lips; extra limbs; merged bodies.
Too many or too few fingers, odd finger spreading, eyes with unusual reflections, distorted ears.
Extra fingers named among common errors.

patterns.notes: Counter-evidence: socialmediaexaminer-generic-ai-images (2026-08-11) reports six-fingered hands as largely gone from current models. The research guide already shows subtler cases (a thumb that appears detached, an implausible knee) alongside the obvious ones.

patterns.name: Averaged idealized face
patterns.summary: People get generically beautiful faces averaged out of many: symmetric, ageless, conventionally attractive, in proportion, without distinguishing marks, and in groups they resemble one another. Research on synthetic faces finds them more average and more in proportion than real faces, with attractiveness a usable cue; practitioner sources list the generic face as a current default. The result is a cast of interchangeable people.

detector.rubric: Look at each prominent human face. Flag the image if the faces are idealized and interchangeable: high symmetry, smooth proportions, no distinguishing marks (asymmetry, scars, moles, crooked teeth, irregular noses, wrinkles fitting the stated or apparent age), model-like attractiveness whatever the role, and in group images faces that share the same features apart from skin tone or hair. Count one hit per image. Does not count: professional models in fashion or beauty contexts; illustration or animation styles that idealize faces by convention; faces too small or distant to judge; a single attractive person whose features are still specific and irregular. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Stock-style image of a construction crew in which all five workers have flawless symmetric faces, perfect teeth and the same model-like features.
Portrait captioned 'a 70-year-old fisherman' showing a face with hardly any wrinkles, symmetric features and the look of a fashion model.
Group photo of a startup team in which the faces differ in skin tone and hair but share the same nose, jaw and eye shape.
negative: Portrait of a man with a crooked nose, a scar on his chin, uneven eyebrows and deep crow's feet.
Fashion campaign image of a professional model, where idealized beauty is the brief.
Wide shot of a stadium crowd in which faces are too small to assess.

patterns.legitimate_use: Fashion, beauty and casting contexts that ask for model looks, and illustration styles that idealize faces by convention.
patterns.fix: Re-cast: give each person specific, irregular features that fit age and role (asymmetry, wrinkles, scars, moles, glasses, a gap between the teeth, different face shapes) and vary them across a group. Keep idealized beauty for contexts where it is the point.
patterns.prevention: Describe people as individuals: age, build and a couple of specific features ("a broad face with a crooked nose and deep smile lines", "freckles and a chipped front tooth"). For groups, state that faces, ages and body types differ. Ask for model looks only when the brief is about fashion or beauty.

sources.note: 'symmetrical, ageless, conventionally attractive', 'a face averaged out of a thousand other faces'.
AI faces (StyleGAN2) judged human more often than real faces; 'more in-proportion'.
AI faces 'more average (and therefore less distinctive)'; attractiveness a correct cue. Derived from the paper.
Idealized, beautiful people.

patterns.notes: The peer-reviewed evidence concerns GAN face synthesis; applying it to diffusion output is an inference that the image benchmark should test.

patterns.name: Centered symmetric hero composition
patterns.summary: The subject stands dead center, frontal and often mirror-symmetric, looking into the lens, with nothing that leads the eye elsewhere. Practitioner sources describe it as the fallback when a prompt gives no composition guidance. Centering is a valid choice for formal portraits, icons and symmetric architecture; the pattern is centering that nobody chose.

detector.rubric: Check the framing. Flag the image if the main subject sits in the central area of the frame, seen straight on at eye level, the composition is close to mirror-symmetric or static, and nothing in the subject, the format or the brief motivates that framing. Typical signs: a person square to the lens in the exact middle; an object floating centered on a plain or radial background; a glowing focal element in the middle of a symmetric scene. Count one hit per image. Does not count: passport, ID, catalog or icon images whose format requires centering; architecture or interiors photographed along their axis of symmetry; formal portraits where the frontal pose is the point; centered images that use depth, an unusual crop or angle, or a secondary subject to create tension. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Blog image on remote work: a smiling woman with a laptop exactly in the middle of the frame, square to the camera, identical bookshelves on both sides, shot at eye level.
Concept image for 'innovation': a glowing lightbulb dead center on a symmetric dark radial background with nothing else in the frame.
Fantasy warrior standing front-on in the middle of the image, arms at the sides, symmetric mountains behind, looking straight into the lens.
negative: Street photo with the subject walking out of the right third of the frame, shot from a low angle, a passing bus blurred on the left.
Shop catalog image of a water bottle centered on white, as the catalog format requires.
Photo of a cathedral nave taken from the central aisle along the building's axis of symmetry.

patterns.legitimate_use: Formats that need a centered subject (catalog, ID, icon), symmetric architecture, formal portraiture and symmetry used as a deliberate design idea.
patterns.fix: Recompose: move the subject onto a third or toward an edge, change camera height or angle, crop tighter or wider, add a foreground element or a secondary subject, or let the subject look or move out of frame. Keep centering only where the format needs it.
patterns.prevention: State the composition: where the subject sits in the frame (left third, lower right), camera height and angle (low angle, over the shoulder, top-down), crop and lens, and what the subject is doing instead of posing ("caught mid-task, looking at the workbench"). Ask for centered symmetry only for formats that require it.

sources.note: 'the subject squarely in the middle of the frame', 'weirdly static'.
'Without composition guidance, the model defaults to a straight-on, centered shot.'

patterns.name: Default cinematic lighting
patterns.summary: The scene is dramatized with movie-still light regardless of what it shows: warm low-sun backlight, a glowing rim around the subject, haze and light shafts, theatrical contrast. The research guide calls it cinematization; practitioner sources describe golden-hour light applied whether or not the place and time of day could produce it. The look is generic because it ignores the light the depicted location would have.

detector.rubric: Decide whether the lighting is motivated by the depicted setting. Flag the image if it applies dramatic cinematic lighting that the scene gives no reason for: warm low-sun backlight or a golden glow in an indoor, overcast or midday setting; a rim light outlining the subject with no visible or plausible source; haze, light shafts, lens flares or floating dust in an everyday scene such as an office, kitchen or classroom; theatrical contrast that turns a mundane activity into a film still. Count one hit per image. Does not count: scenes set at sunrise or sunset, in fog, at a concert or on a stage, where light direction and color agree with the setting; briefs that are explicitly cinematic (film poster, game key art, album cover); graded images whose light sources stay physically consistent with the scene. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Stock-style image of two colleagues at a laptop in an open-plan office, backlit by a warm orange glow with light shafts through haze, although the windows show an overcast sky.
Portrait of a nurse in a hospital corridor with a bright golden rim light around her hair and shoulders and no lamp or window behind her.
Image of a person reading at a kitchen table, lit like a film poster with deep shadows, a lens flare and dust particles glowing in the beams.
negative: Photo of hikers on a ridge at sunset, warm low light coming from the visible sun on the horizon and long shadows pointing away from it.
Office meeting under ceiling fluorescents with even, slightly cool light and soft shadows under the desks.
Film poster key art with a hero backlit by an explosion, where the brief is a poster.

patterns.legitimate_use: Film posters, game key art and album covers, and scenes that are really set at golden hour, in fog or under stage light. The finding concerns light that the setting does not motivate.
patterns.fix: Relight to match the depicted place and time. Name the real source (a window on the left, ceiling fluorescents, an overcast sky, a desk lamp) and let its color and direction govern every shadow; remove haze, flares and rim light that have no source; lower contrast to what the setting would produce.
patterns.prevention: Specify the light source, its direction and its color temperature for the actual setting and time of day, for example "flat overcast daylight from a window on the left" or "cool overhead fluorescent light with soft shadows under the desk". Ask for golden hour, rim light, haze or light shafts only when the scene is set where they occur or the brief is explicitly cinematic.

sources.note: Generated images 'often portray a cinematic or picturesque style that dramatizes the subjects'; caveat that real photography uses the same style.
'Overly cinematic-looking backgrounds'.
Lighting described as 'dramatic'.
'The contrast is too high'.

patterns.name: Cybersecurity imagery clichés
patterns.summary: Security and hacking topics are illustrated with a hooded figure hunched over a laptop, often masked or in a balaclava, green Matrix-style ones and zeros on black, glowing padlocks or shields over circuit boards, and dark rooms lit by screens. A foundation-run design challenge (based on interviews with security experts and visual creators), a newsroom handbook and a stock photographer's account document the set and describe it as misleading about the people and the work involved.

detector.rubric: First decide whether the image illustrates cybersecurity, hacking, privacy, fraud or data protection. If it does, flag it when its main motif is one of these: a hooded, masked or faceless figure at a keyboard or laptop; streams of binary digits or green code on a dark background; a glowing padlock, shield or keyhole floating over circuitry or a keyboard; a skull or warning symbol on a screen in a dark room. Count one hit per image. Does not count: photos of real security work (an analyst at a monitoring desk, a team in an incident meeting, a person using a hardware key); real screenshots of phishing emails or warning dialogs; a padlock icon used as an interface element in a UI mockup. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Article image on ransomware: a hooded figure with no visible face typing on a laptop in a dark room, green binary code reflected on the screen.
A glowing blue padlock floating above a circuit board with streams of ones and zeros.
Illustration for a password guide: a figure in a balaclava holding a credit card in front of a monitor that shows a red skull.
negative: Photo of an IT administrator in a bright office pressing a hardware security key into a laptop.
Screenshot of a real phishing email with the suspicious link highlighted.
Login screen mockup with a small padlock icon next to the password field.

patterns.legitimate_use: Real security work, real artifacts such as phishing mails, warning dialogs and hardware keys, interface icons, and knowing parody of the clichés.
patterns.fix: Show the concrete threat or defense and the people affected: the employee reading a suspicious invoice email, the help-desk call, the update screen on a hospital computer, the analyst's monitoring dashboard. Replace the faceless attacker with the consequence or the defense.
patterns.prevention: For security topics, describe the real situation and the people in it, for example "a clinic receptionist hesitates over an email asking her to reset a password, bright daytime office". Ask for hooded or masked figures, binary or green code, glowing padlocks or shields only when the brief is about that imagery.

sources.note: Men in hoodies, sometimes with burglar masks, looming over keyboards; green Matrix-style 1s and 0s; glowing locks and server racks.
'a dark hooded figure leaning menacingly over a laptop'; padlock surrounded by Matrix typography; balaclava.
Hooded anonymous figures on keyboards, closed locks, glowing green leetspeak on dark backgrounds, a maze of binary. Funded by the same foundation as hewlett-cybersecurity-imagery.

patterns.notes: The sources document the stock-imagery cliché. Over-representation in image-model output relative to human-made illustrations is untested and is the question for the image benchmark.

patterns.name: Default color grade
patterns.summary: Colors follow a generator default instead of the subject: saturation and contrast pushed hard, an orange-and-teal split, or a uniform yellow, amber or sepia cast over the whole frame. Reported for Midjourney and Ideogram (orange and teal, stronger on abstract prompts), for ChatGPT image generation (yellow cast, 2025) and for generators in general (oversaturation). Each palette is a legitimate grading choice; the pattern is its appearance by default.

detector.rubric: Judge the overall color treatment. Flag the image if one of these dominates without a reason in the subject or the brief: saturation and contrast pushed so far that reds read as neon, blues as electric and skin as orange; an orange-and-teal split where warm highlights and skin sit against cyan or teal shadows and backgrounds in a scene that contains no such colors; a yellow, amber or sepia cast that tints whites, skies and neutral surfaces across the whole frame. Count one hit per image. Does not count: scenes whose real colors produce the palette (sunset over the sea, a teal wall, tungsten-lit interiors); a grade the brief asks for (period look, film emulation, brand palette); monochrome or duotone design; images in which neutral whites stay neutral. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Image of a pianist on stage in which every highlight and skin tone is orange and every shadow and wall is teal, although the hall has white walls and wooden panels.
Illustration of a city street in which the whole frame, including white shirts and the sky, carries a uniform yellow-sepia tint like an old print, with no period brief.
Landscape image with neon-green grass, an electric-blue sky and orange skin tones, contrast so high that the shadows turn solid black.
negative: Photo of a beach at sunset where the orange sky and the blue-green sea are the real colors of the scene.
Product photo on a white background in which white stays neutral and the packaging colors match the real product.
Sepia-toned image for a magazine feature on the 1920s, where the brief asks for a period look.

patterns.legitimate_use: Color grading is a craft choice. Orange and teal, warm vintage tints and saturated palettes are legitimate when the brief or the scene asks for them. Flag only a grade that appears regardless of subject, which practitioners report most often on short or abstract prompts.
patterns.fix: Re-grade from neutral: set white balance on something known to be neutral (a white shirt, paper, a grey wall), pull saturation back until skin reads natural, remove the global tint, then apply a palette chosen for the subject or the brand if one is wanted.
patterns.prevention: Name the palette and the white balance in the prompt, either generically ("neutral white balance, true-to-life colors, muted saturation") or concretely ("sage green, off-white and charcoal", "cool blue-grey winter light"). Give a full scene description, since short abstract prompts leave color to the default. Ask for a vintage tint or an orange-and-teal grade only when the brief calls for it.

sources.note: Orange-and-teal bias in Midjourney and Ideogram, stronger on abstract prompts.
User reports of a yellow or sepia cast in ChatGPT image output; derived_from flitto-orange-teal-bias.
'the color saturation cranked to 11'.
Colors 'bright and saturated'.
'excessive saturation'.

patterns.name: Dysfunctional objects and dissolving detail
patterns.summary: Objects look plausible at a glance and fail on inspection: a watch growing out of an arm, a broom with an unusable grip, a detached racket handle, stairs leading into a wall, guitar strings in varying numbers, a backpack strap turning into a shirt, background crowds whose faces dissolve, repeating background patterns. The image renders what objects look like without how they work.

detector.rubric: Check each object and how it is used. Flag the image if an object could not work as depicted (handles detached or fused, tools with impossible grips, furniture blocking its own use, stairs or doors leading nowhere, instruments with irregular strings or keys); if objects merge into each other or into people; if a person holds or uses something in a way that cannot work (a sandwich held edge-on, a hand inside a burger); or if background detail dissolves on close view (smeared faces in a crowd, repeating or melting patterns, nonsensical architecture). Count one hit per image. Does not count: unusual but real designs (avant-garde fashion, historic architecture); objects too small or too far out of focus to resolve in an otherwise coherent image; deliberate surreal art. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Image of a man checking a wristwatch that grows out of his forearm, its face showing lines instead of numbers.
Photo-style kitchen in which the oven door and the stovetop merge into one object and the cupboard handles float beside the doors.
Street scene in which the people in the background have smeared, melted faces and every shop front repeats the same window.
negative: Photo of a jacket with oversized buckles from a designer runway collection.
Portrait with an out-of-focus crowd behind the subject, faces softened by depth of field but shaped like faces.
Surrealist painting of a melting clock presented as surrealism.

patterns.legitimate_use: Surreal art and real but unusual designs. Softness from depth of field is optical and does not count.
patterns.fix: Inspect props one by one and replace or inpaint any object that could not work; reduce the number of props; keep backgrounds sparse and coherent, or blur them deliberately; correct the action so the grip and contact are physically possible.
patterns.prevention: Keep scenes sparse and name the few props that matter together with their function ("an analog wristwatch with a leather strap on her left wrist", "holding a broom by its handle with both hands"). Describe background people as few and distant, or ask for an empty background when a crowd adds nothing. Inspect props and background at full size before use.

sources.locator: section 03 Functional Implausibilities (3.1 to 3.3), 3.3 crowd faces
sources.note: Floating or merging objects, dysfunctional objects (watch emerging from the arm, broken broom grip, detached racket handle), glitched detail, uncanny small faces in crowds.
'a hand inside a hamburger'.
Backgrounds repetitive or nonsensical; impossible details such as oversized flowers on a hat.

patterns.name: Light, shadow and perspective inconsistency
patterns.summary: The scene breaks optics and geometry: shadows point in different directions or are missing, reflections show a different scene, perspective lines fail to converge, stairs climb and descend at once, and the subject is lit differently from the background as if pasted in. The research guide lists these as violations of physics and as inconsistencies of resolution and color.

detector.rubric: Trace light and geometry. Flag the image if shadows from one light source point in different directions, are missing under objects that should cast them, or have shapes unlike their objects; if mirrors, water or glossy surfaces reflect something that differs from the scene (other clothing, another pose, extra limbs); if parallel lines such as floors, roads or shelves converge inconsistently, straight lines warp, or paths and stairs are geometrically impossible; or if a subject's light direction, color temperature or sharpness differs from the background as in a cut-out composite. Count one hit per image. Does not count: several real light sources that explain several shadow directions; distortion from wide-angle or fisheye lenses; deliberate surreal or optical-illusion images; photomontage that presents itself as montage. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Image of three people on a sunny sidewalk whose shadows fall behind them while the shadow of the tree beside them falls to the left.
A man in a short-sleeved shirt stands in front of a mirror, and his reflection wears a long-sleeved jacket.
Portrait of a runner lit from the left, placed on a stadium background lit from the right and rendered sharper than the runner.
negative: Night street scene with two street lamps producing two consistent shadows per person.
Wide-angle interior photo with the curved edges typical of the lens.
Impossible-staircase illustration made as a deliberate optical illusion and presented as art.

patterns.legitimate_use: Surreal and optical-illusion art, montage that announces itself, and multi-light setups that explain several shadows.
patterns.fix: Choose one key light and correct every shadow, highlight and reflection to it; rebuild reflections from the actual scene; straighten lines so they share vanishing points; match the subject's light direction, color temperature and sharpness to the background, or rebuild the composite.
patterns.prevention: Describe the light source and its direction once and keep the scene simple enough for it to govern, for example "late-afternoon sun from the right, long shadows falling to the left". Use mirrors, water reflections and complex staircases only when the image needs them, and then describe what the reflection shows. Ask for one consistent camera position and lens.

sources.locator: section 04 Violations of Physics (4.1 to 4.3) and 2.4 Inconsistencies in Resolution & Color
sources.note: Shadows in inconsistent directions, reflections inconsistent with the scene, depth and perspective warping; subjects that look pasted onto backgrounds.
'shadows often defy the laws of physics'.
Background lighting unlike the foreground; shadows in different directions or absent; perspective inconsistent or wrong.

patterns.name: Plastic skin and surface texture
patterns.summary: Skin rendered waxy, poreless or glossy, and materials such as fabric, food, wood or stone rendered as uniformly smooth surfaces with a soft specular sheen. Image generators drift toward this idealized smoothness when a prompt leaves texture open; retouched fashion and product photography shows the same finish by choice, so the pattern is the finish appearing where the image claims documentary realism.

detector.rubric: Look at every visible area of human skin and at the main material surfaces. Flag the image if skin lacks pores, fine lines, fine hair and tonal variation and reads as wax, resin, vinyl or a 3D render, or if it carries an even, oily highlight that the scene lighting does not explain. Also flag it when fabrics, food, wood or stone show no fine texture and share one uniform glossy finish. Count one hit per image. Does not count: a deliberate stylization (cartoon, 3D animation, clay or toy look) that the whole image commits to; retouched skin in an image that is plainly a beauty, fashion or product advertisement and keeps texture elsewhere; low-resolution or heavily compressed images where texture cannot be judged; surfaces that are genuinely glossy (wet skin, lacquer, polished metal, glass) with highlights consistent with the light sources. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Close-up portrait of a middle-aged man whose cheeks and forehead show no pores or wrinkles, the skin uniformly smooth with a soft sheen like polished resin, while his beard is drawn strand by strand.
Product shot of a knitted sweater on a table: the knit shows no loops or fuzz, and the wool looks like molded plastic with a glossy highlight along every fold.
Photo-style image of a farmer in a dusty field at midday whose face is flawless, poreless and evenly glowing, unlike the harsh light on everything around him.
negative: Candid street photo of an elderly woman with visible pores, age spots and fine wrinkles under flat overcast light.
Stylized 3D animated character with smooth vinyl skin, consistent with the toy-like style of the whole frame.
Studio advertisement for foundation makeup with retouched skin, where hair, fabric and background keep natural texture and the retouching is the product message.

patterns.legitimate_use: Beauty and cosmetics advertising, fashion editorials and stylized 3D or toy-like illustration use smooth skin on purpose. Report a finding only when the smoothness contradicts the register the image claims, for example a documentary scene, a portrait meant to look candid, or a product whose material should be visible.
patterns.fix: Restore texture wherever the image claims realism. Retouch or re-render skin with pores, fine lines, peach fuzz, uneven tone and small blemishes; give fabric its weave, food its crumbs and wood its grain; reduce specular highlights to those the light sources justify. If the smooth finish is the intent, commit to a clearly stylized medium across the whole frame.
patterns.prevention: When a photographic look is wanted, describe skin and materials explicitly: natural skin texture with visible pores, fine lines and uneven tone, no retouching or beauty filter; name each material texture ("coarse wool knit", "matte unglazed ceramic", "scuffed leather"). State a light quality that keeps texture visible, such as soft side light or overcast daylight. Ask for smooth, glossy finishes only when the brief is a stylized 3D or advertising look.

sources.note: Skin texture of generated people 'waxy, shiny, cartoonish, or glossy'; caveat that fashion photos also show perfect skin.
'The skin might be waxy and shiny'.
Skin 'often lacks pores or appears overly polished'; fabrics lack fine mesh detail.
'very glossy', 'as smooth as a Barbie doll', 'a certain plasticity'.
Surfaces 'blurred or airbrushed'.

patterns.notes: Counter-evidence: socialmediaexaminer-generic-ai-images (2026-08-11) reports plastic-looking skin as largely gone from current models. The image benchmark should measure the rate on current output before any promotion.

patterns.name: Prompt overfitting
patterns.summary: One attribute from the prompt leaks into parts of the image where it does not belong: stripes asked for on shirts reappear on the wallpaper, one face is duplicated across several people, a theme color bleeds into hems, laces and props. Documented in one research guide; kept as an observation until a second independent source is registered.

detector.rubric: Compare the image with its evident subject, and with the prompt if one is available. Flag it if a single attribute (a pattern, color, object or face) repeats across unrelated parts of the scene in a way real scenes rarely show: the same stripe pattern on clothes, walls and furniture; one face on several people; a theme color bleeding into hems, props and background. Count one hit per image. Does not count: coordinated designs where repetition is intended (team uniforms, branded event decor, matching outfits); twins; repeating architecture. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Image of a group of kids in striped shirts standing in front of wallpaper with the same stripes, next to a striped sofa.
Office scene in which the same woman's face appears on three different people around the table.
Image of a student in a purple university hoodie where purple also shows up on the frayed edges of black jeans and on the shoelaces.
negative: Photo of a football team in identical striped jerseys during a match.
Photo of identical twins sitting side by side.
Branded conference stage where the logo color repeats on banners by design.

patterns.legitimate_use: Intended repetition: uniforms, matching outfits, branded decor, twins, repeating architecture.
patterns.fix: Regenerate with each attribute bound to its object ("only the shirts are striped; plain white wall"), inpaint stray repetitions, and check the faces in groups for duplicates.
patterns.prevention: Bind each attribute to its object and describe the other elements explicitly, for example "the children wear striped shirts; the wall behind them is plain white; each child has a different face, age and hairstyle".

sources.note: Stripes from 'kids wearing striped shirts' overrepresented in the wallpaper; a person apparently cloned; university colors on frayed denim.

patterns.name: Pseudo-text and malformed lettering
patterns.summary: Lettering in the image is glyph-like nonsense, misspelled or missing letters, switches font inside a word, wanders off its baseline, or uses a typeface the object would never carry; fake logos imitate brand marks without being any brand. Text rendering has improved, so the errors have moved from obvious gibberish toward almost-right typography that still breaks on a close read.

detector.rubric: Read every piece of text in the image: signs, labels, screens, clothing, packaging, logos and numbers. Flag the image if any text is illegible glyph-like shapes or a nonexistent language; if a real word is misspelled or missing letters; if letters change font, weight or size inside a word; if kerning is irregular or baselines wander; if the same symbol is rendered differently within one graphic; or if a logo-like mark resembles a brand but reads as nonsense. Also flag a typeface that is implausible for the object, such as a script font on a university sweatshirt. Count one hit per image. Does not count: text that is legible and correct; text intentionally blurred, out of focus or too small to read; invented scripts in fantasy or science-fiction art that the brief asks for; real brand logos rendered correctly. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Image of a café storefront whose sign reads 'COFEFE BARISTAH' in letters that change from serif to sans-serif halfway through.
Infographic in which the percent signs and digits change shape from one statistic to the next and the headline baseline wavers.
Street scene with shop signs full of letter-like shapes that form no language and a logo resembling a sportswear swoosh fused with a letter.
negative: Photo of a street sign that reads 'Main St' clearly and correctly.
Shallow-focus photo in which a distant poster is blurred beyond reading.
Fantasy map with an invented runic script requested in the brief.

patterns.legitimate_use: Invented scripts in fiction, deliberate glitch typography, and text that is out of focus by design.
patterns.fix: Remove generated text and set real type in a layout tool, or regenerate with the exact wording; replace fake logos with real assets used with permission or with neutral surfaces; proofread spelling, kerning and the consistency of repeated symbols.
patterns.prevention: Either give the exact wording in quotes with font style and placement ("the words 'Open Daily' in bold condensed sans-serif on the awning"), or ask for surfaces free of text and logos and add typography later in a layout tool. Request a brand logo only when the image is allowed to use it, and supply the real asset.

sources.note: Glyph-like text in nonexistent languages, nonexistent words, spelling errors; perfect text in an unconventional font for a sweatshirt.
Letters 'warped, stretched or twisted'; font switches within one word or sentence.
Inconsistent kerning, baselines, letter shapes and stroke weights; the same percent sign rendered differently.
Images with illegible characters.

patterns.notes: openart-visual-cliches (2026-05) states that current models render legible text well; the pattern now targets almost-right typography and fake logos as much as gibberish.

patterns.name: Quality-tag prompt stacking
patterns.summary: Image prompts built from stacked generic quality and platform tags ("hyperrealistic, 8k, masterpiece, best quality, highly detailed, trending on artstation, unreal engine") in place of a description of the scene. The habit comes from early diffusion communities, where such quality boosters were taught as standard practice; current vendor guidance asks for narrative scene descriptions, and practitioners report that the tags add little on current models. The pattern lives in the prompt, and its visible result is the generic default look covered by the other image patterns.

detector.rubric: Evaluate the generation prompt when it is available together with the image (supplied by the user, stored in the image metadata, or written by you before generating). Flag it if the prompt relies on generic quality or platform tags instead of describing the scene: two or more terms such as "masterpiece", "best quality", "high quality", "8k", "4k", "ultra HD", "hyperrealistic", "hyper-detailed", "highly detailed", "intricate", "trending on artstation", "award-winning", "octane render", "unreal engine", "epic" or "stunning", typically as a comma-separated list appended to a short subject. Count one hit per prompt. Does not count: one technical term that serves the brief (an output resolution required by a print specification, a game-engine look for a game asset); camera, lens, film stock, medium or lighting terms that describe how the image is made; prompts that describe the scene in full sentences and add a single quality word. If no prompt is available, list the pattern as not evaluated.

positive: Prompt: 'woman in a cafe, masterpiece, best quality, 8k, hyperrealistic, highly detailed, trending on artstation'.
Prompt: 'futuristic city, epic, stunning, ultra HD, octane render, unreal engine, award-winning'.
Prompt: 'portrait of an old fisherman, 4k, intricate, hyper-detailed, masterpiece'.
negative: Prompt: 'An elderly fisherman mends a net on a wooden pier at dawn; flat grey light, 50mm lens at eye level, muted blues and browns, his hands in sharp focus.'
Prompt: 'Poster artwork at 300 dpi for an A2 print: a hand-drawn map of the old town in ink and watercolor.'
Prompt: 'Product photo of a ceramic mug on a linen tablecloth, soft window light from the left, shot on 35mm film.'

patterns.legitimate_use: Technical output requirements such as print resolution or aspect ratio, and concrete capture or medium descriptions such as lens, film stock or ink and watercolor, are specifications. They do not count as quality tags.
patterns.fix: Rewrite the prompt as a scene description covering subject and action, setting, composition and camera position, light source and time of day, palette, and medium. Delete the generic quality and platform tags and regenerate.
patterns.prevention: Write image prompts as a short descriptive paragraph that names subject and action, setting, composition, light, palette and medium. Replace every generic quality or platform tag ("masterpiece", "8k", "hyperrealistic", "highly detailed", "trending on artstation") with the concrete property it was meant to produce: a lens, a light source, a texture, a medium.

sources.locator: principle 'Describe the scene, don't just list keywords'
sources.note: Narrative description yields more coherent images than disconnected words; use camera, lens and lighting terms.
Quality tags waste token budget and confuse composition; current models already default to high quality.
Documents 'trending on artstation', 'masterpiece', 'highly detailed', 'rendered in Unreal Engine' as community quality boosters; prevalence evidence.
Teaches 4K, 8K, masterpiece, best quality, hyper-detailed; prevalence evidence only.

patterns.notes: Prompt-level pattern. The vision rubric applies to the prompt that accompanies an image and to prompts the host model writes in prevent mode; an image audit without a prompt reports it under not evaluated. The realization examples are prompts, which is the input this detector reads.

patterns.name: Stereotyped default people
patterns.summary: When a prompt names a role, a nationality or a generic person without further description, generators fill in a narrow stereotype: doctors and leaders as white men, "an Indian person" as an old bearded man in a turban, a Mexican person in a sombrero, American scenes with a flag, women younger and lighter-skinned than men. Studies of Midjourney, Kandinsky, Firefly and other text-to-image models find the outputs uniform and report amplified racial and gender disparities.

detector.rubric: Look at the people and cultural markers in relation to the image's topic. Flag the image if the people follow a narrow demographic or cultural stereotype for their role or origin that the brief does not require: every person in a high-status role is a white man; every person in a care or service role is a woman or a person of color; a nationality is reduced to costume clichés (turban, sombrero, national flag), poverty markers or folkloric dress in an everyday scene; a group is uniform in age, body type and skin tone where variety would be expected. Count one hit per image. Does not count: images of specific real people or events; briefs that specify the demographics; traditional dress at an occasion where it is worn; a single person depicted with specific individual features and context. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Image for 'a doctor talking to a nurse': an older white male doctor and a young female nurse, the same casting in every variant.
Image for 'a person from India' showing an elderly man with a long beard and a turban in a dusty street, although the prompt named no age, gender or setting.
Image for 'a family dinner in the USA' with a US flag standing on the table and printed on the plates.
negative: Photo of surgeons of different genders, ages and skin tones working together in an operating room.
Image requested as 'an elderly Sikh man at a gurdwara', shown wearing a turban as the brief specifies.
Photo of a Mexican office worker in business clothes at a laptop in a Mexico City office.

patterns.legitimate_use: Briefs that specify who is shown, documentation of specific people or events, and traditional dress at occasions where it is worn.
patterns.fix: Re-cast deliberately: decide age, gender, skin tone, body type and dress for each person according to the setting and its real population, and remove costume or flag markers whose only job is to signal nationality. Show contemporary everyday settings for any country.
patterns.prevention: Define the people whenever a role or an origin could invite a stereotype: give each person an age, gender, appearance and clothing that fit the real setting ("a woman in her forties in a lab coat and a young man in scrubs"). Describe contemporary everyday settings for every country, and include flags or folkloric costume only when the occasion calls for them.

sources.note: About 3,000 Midjourney images; 'an Indian person' 99 of 100 men, 92 with headwear; 'a Mexican person' 99 of 100 with a sombrero or similar hat; all 100 American images with a flag.
Trait and role prompts reinforce whiteness as ideal; occupations amplify racial and gender disparities; stereotypes persist against counter-stereotypical prompting.
Midjourney presidential candidates all white, male, American; doctors as white men in 1950s style.

patterns.name: Uniform hyper-detail
patterns.summary: Fine detail is spread evenly over the whole image or piled up where no viewer would look: intricate ornament on every surface, strand-by-strand windswept hair in a still scene, filigree on clothing and props. With no area of rest the image has no focal hierarchy. The research guide describes locally excessive hyper-real detail; practitioner sources describe busy maximalism with nothing emphasized.

detector.rubric: Assess how detail is distributed. Flag the image if intricate detail covers most surfaces at the same intensity so that no area offers visual rest and the subject does not stand out, or if one element (hair, fur, fabric, ornament) shows fine detail that clashes with the rest of the image, for example individually rendered windswept hair in an otherwise still, softly rendered scene. Count one hit per image. Does not count: subjects that are intricate in reality (a baroque altar, a coral reef, a crowded market stall) where the detail follows the subject; deliberately maximalist formats chosen by the brief (fantasy maps, hidden-object puzzles, ornamental pattern design); macro photography of textures. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Fantasy portrait in which armor, background walls, sky and floor are all covered in equally intricate filigree, so the face does not stand out from anything.
Photo-style image of a man standing still in a calm office whose hair is rendered as thousands of fine strands blowing in a strong wind while nothing else moves.
Book cover illustration where every part of the frame holds gears, vines, gems and patterns at the same density.
negative: Photo of a gothic cathedral facade, intricate because the building is.
Portrait with a sharply detailed face against a plain, softly blurred wall.
Hidden-object puzzle illustration whose purpose is dense detail.

patterns.legitimate_use: Intricate real subjects, ornamental design, hidden-object and map illustrations, and maximalist styles that the brief asks for.
patterns.fix: Decide the focal point and reduce detail elsewhere: simplify the background, give large areas a plain material or negative space, calm hair and fabric to match the motion in the scene, and keep the finest detail where the eye should land first.
patterns.prevention: Name one focal point and describe the rest of the frame as calm, for example "simple, uncluttered background with negative space", "plain painted wall", "hair tied back and still". Describe only the details that matter for the subject in place of generic boosters such as "intricate", "highly detailed" or "hyper-detailed".

sources.note: 'intricate patterns on every surface', 'a busy maximalism with no rest for the eye'.
Unnatural detail in specific parts, e.g. hair 'excessively soft, fine-grained and windswept' inconsistent with the scene.

patterns.name: Unmotivated shallow focus
patterns.summary: A creamy blurred background and heavy bokeh behind subjects that would not be photographed that way: wide scenes where the setting matters, groups in which people at the same distance are unevenly sharp, everyday snapshots. Practitioner sources list cinema-grade bokeh as a cliché, and detection guides note blur that masks unresolved detail.

detector.rubric: Compare depth of field with the shot. Flag the image if the background or foreground is strongly blurred with smooth bokeh although framing, distance or purpose call for deep focus: environmental or wide shots where the setting carries the story; group scenes in which people at a similar distance are unevenly sharp; documentary or everyday snapshots; areas where the blur hides incoherent detail such as hands, objects or crowds. Count one hit per image. Does not count: close portraits, macro shots and product detail shots where shallow focus is the usual choice and the blur increases gradually with distance; sports and wildlife shots made with long lenses; briefs that ask for the effect. Describe the visible pattern only; do not infer how the image was made.

positive: Image of a team in a workshop where the person in front is sharp and a colleague at the same table one meter behind dissolves into creamy bokeh.
Image meant to show a village market in which a single apple is in focus and the whole square is reduced to soft discs of light.
Portrait in which the subject is sharp while the book she holds in front of her is smeared by blur that cuts off at its edges.
negative: Close headshot taken with a portrait lens, background softly out of focus with gradual falloff.
Landscape photo of a valley, sharp from the rocks in the foreground to the distant peaks.
Wildlife photo of a heron taken with a long telephoto lens, background blurred by distance.

patterns.legitimate_use: Portraits, macro work, product details, sports and wildlife photography, where shallow depth of field is the normal optical result.
patterns.fix: Increase depth of field so the setting reads (smaller aperture, wider lens); let blur grow with distance; keep people at the same distance equally sharp; if the blur was hiding broken detail, repair that detail and show it.
patterns.prevention: State the depth of field the image needs: "deep focus, background sharp and readable", "f/8, sharp from the table to the far wall", or for a portrait "85mm at f/2.8, background slightly soft". Ask for strong bokeh only for close portraits and product details.

sources.note: 'a creamy blurred background behind subjects that would never actually be shot that way', 'cinema-grade bokeh'.
Backgrounds overly blurred.
'an unnatural amount of blur that appears to mask out the hand and book'.

patterns.name: Anaphora run
patterns.summary: Three or more consecutive sentences open with the same words ("They assume that users will pay. They assume that developers will build. They assume that ecosystems will emerge."). The repeated opening supplies rhythm in place of connection: the sentences are lined up instead of related, and the reader hears a speech where an argument should be.

positive: They assume that users will pay. They assume that developers will build. They assume that ecosystems will emerge.
They have built engines, but not vehicles. They have built power, but not leverage. They have built walls, but not doors.
We believe in speed. We believe in craft. We believe in each other.
Great leaders listen first. Great leaders admit mistakes. Great leaders give credit away.
negative: He opened the box. He checked the seal. He logged the time.
They assume that users will pay. Developers, they say, will build. Ecosystems will follow.
We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields.
In 2019 we moved to Berlin. In 2021 we moved to Lisbon. In 2023 we came back.
The report is late. The report is incomplete. Nobody has read it.

patterns.legitimate_use: Anaphora is a classical figure; speeches, sermons, manifestos and poems use it deliberately, and step-by-step instructions repeat openings for clarity ("Add the flour. Add the sugar. Add the eggs."), which the detector also matches. Flag the run in expository or promotional prose where the repetition replaces the logical links between the sentences.
patterns.fix: Merge the parallel sentences into one statement, or keep one and say how the others relate to it (cause, contrast, sequence). If the repetition is meant as a figure, use it once in the text and make the last item the strongest.
patterns.prevention: Do not start three sentences in a row with the same words. Connect the ideas with content, not with a repeated opening.
patterns.notes: Mechanism: sentence-level repetition of the opening words across consecutive sentences. Closest existing patterns: triad (three-item coordinations inside a sentence) and antithesis-template (a denial followed by an assertion). The anaphora run works across sentence boundaries and needs no contrast; the tropes-fyi example "They have built engines, but not vehicles. ..." combines all three. The detector requires the same first two words in three consecutive sentences, so a narrative run with the same pronoun but different verbs ("He opened ... He checked ...") does not match; the humanizer skill flags those single-subject runs too, which a regex cannot separate from normal narration. Two-word openers that repeat in instructions produce false positives (see legitimate_use). Status: kept as observation although the validator counts two clusters. The Wikipedia guide has no anaphora entry, so neither source copies it here, but skill-humanizer is derived from that guide and the guide's source record names tropes-fyi as part of the same lineage; no third source with no tie to either is known (the Deslop skill mentions "anaphora/tricolon abuse" but links a tropes catalog).

sources.locator: entry 'Anaphora abuse', category Sentence Structure, directory status fading
sources.note: "Repeating the same sentence opening multiple times in quick succession"; examples with runs of "They assume that", "They could" and "They have built".
"Several sentences in a row start with the same subject, often she or he." No counterpart in the Wikipedia guide, which the skill otherwise draws on.

patterns.name: Announce-then-answer preamble
patterns.summary: The text opens by previewing what it is about to do, prefacing the point or restating the question instead of making the point: "In this article, I'll walk you through ...", "Here's what you need to know", "You're asking whether ...". The reader reads a promise before the content.

positive: In this article, I'll walk you through the new billing rules.
Here's what you need to know about the merger.
Before we dive in, a quick word on terminology.
You're asking whether the update is safe to install.
negative: In this article, published in 2019, the author argued for a carbon tax.
Here's what happened: the backup job failed at 02:00.
You're asking the wrong person; the finance team owns that budget.
Before we left, we locked the server room.

positive: In diesem Artikel zeige ich Ihnen die neuen Abrechnungsregeln.
Hier ist, was Sie über die Fusion wissen müssen.
Bevor wir einsteigen, kurz ein Wort zur Terminologie.
Sie fragen, ob das Update sicher installiert werden kann.
negative: In diesem Artikel aus dem Jahr 2019 argumentiert die Autorin für eine CO2-Steuer.
Hier ist der Schlüssel, den du vergessen hast.
Bevor wir gingen, haben wir den Serverraum abgeschlossen.
Sie fragen beim Support nach, wenn die Lieferung ausbleibt.

patterns.legitimate_use: Long guides and course material benefit from a short orientation, and an email reply may restate a question to avoid ambiguity. Flag preambles in short texts and answers where the content could start in the first sentence.
patterns.fix: Delete the preamble and start with the first substantive sentence, usually the answer or the main claim.
patterns.prevention: Do not announce what the text will do or restate the question. Start with the answer or the main point.
patterns.notes: Independent sources: tropes-fyi and pangram-signs-of-ai-writing (phrase multipliers for assistant openers); popularai-ai-tells-2026 describes the same throat-clearing. tropes.fyi also counts announcing the count or shape of what follows ("Two constraints shape the design.") and throat-clearing frames ("The more important point is where the decision itself sits."); the first overlaps compulsive-counting, the second is left to a reader's judgement because the phrases are common in ordinary prose. Close to generic-opening and payoff-announcement but kept separate: the preamble previews the answer or restates the question, while generic-opening frames the world or the present age and payoff-announcement builds suspense before a punchline. Threshold not yet calibrated against the reference corpora.

sources.note: Opening by previewing the output, prefacing the point or restating the prompt. Examples: "Two constraints shape the design.", "The more important point is where the decision itself sits."

patterns.name: Antithesis template
patterns.summary: Negative parallelism that simulates depth by first denying a claim nobody made and then asserting the "real" point ("It's not just X, it's Y"). A disguised variant splits denial and claim into two sentences ("X isn't the point. Instead, Y."; "Das Tool spart keine Zeit. Stattdessen verändert es, wie Teams denken."). Used once as a deliberate contrast it is ordinary rhetoric; produced reflexively it signals template writing.

patterns: (?i)\b(?:isn[’']?t|is not|aren[’']?t|are not|it[’']s not|that[’']s not)\s+(?:just\s+|merely\s+|simply\s+)?about\s+[^.!?\n]{1,60}?[.;,—–-]\s*(?:it[’']?s|it is|they[’']?re|they are|this is)\s+about\b

positive: It's not just a tool — it's a movement.
This isn't about technology. It's about trust.
Not only does it cut costs; it reshapes how teams work.
It's not about speed. It's about trust.
Speed isn't the point. Instead, the real gain is clarity.
The tool doesn't save time. Instead, it changes how teams think.
negative: The fix is not in the parser but in the tokenizer, see issue #12.
Not only the CPU but also the GPU was throttled during the test.
It is not clear whether the patch landed before the freeze.
We did not use Redis. Instead, we cached in memory to save 40 ms.
This method does not modify the list. Instead, it returns a new copy.

positive: Das ist kein Werkzeug, das ist eine Haltung.
Nicht die Technik entscheidet, sondern die Kultur.
Es ist nicht nur ein Update – es ist ein Neuanfang.
Es geht nicht um Technik. Es geht um Vertrauen.
Geschwindigkeit ist nicht der Punkt. Vielmehr geht es um Vertrauen.
Das Tool spart keine Zeit. Stattdessen verändert es, wie Teams denken.
negative: Das Problem liegt nicht am Parser, sondern am Tokenizer.
Die Messung zeigt keine Regression; der Durchsatz bleibt bei 4,2 GB/s.
Es ist nicht nötig, den Dienst neu zu starten.
Wir haben Redis nicht genutzt. Stattdessen cachen wir im Speicher und sparen 40 ms.
Die Methode verändert die Liste nicht. Stattdessen liefert sie eine neue Kopie.

patterns.legitimate_use: A single, substantive correction of a misconception the reader actually holds ("The outage was not caused by the update but by an expired certificate") is not slop. The same holds for the two-sentence form when it reports a concrete decision or behavior and its reason ("We did not use Redis. Instead, we cached in memory to save 40 ms."; "This method does not modify the list. Instead, it returns a new copy."). Flag the reflexive form: the denied claim is a strawman and the text would lose nothing if it only stated the second half. In the disguised form the denial stands as its own short sentence and the next one, opened by "Instead", "Rather", "Stattdessen" or "Vielmehr", reframes the subject in abstract terms.
patterns.fix: State the claim directly without the negation. If a real misconception exists, name it and give the evidence that refutes it.
patterns.prevention: Do not build sentences of the form "not X, but Y" or "it's not just X, it's Y" unless you are correcting a misconception the reader demonstrably holds. State the point directly.

sources.note: Reported at 3x the human baseline (commercial corpus, methodology not disclosed).

patterns.notes: The regexes cover the disguised two-sentence variant only in narrow forms: a "not the point / goal / question" sentence followed by Instead, Rather or a restated point (German: "ist nicht der Punkt", "das Ziel", "die Frage" followed by Stattdessen, Vielmehr or "Es geht um"); "It's not about X. It's about Y." and "Es geht nicht um X. Es geht um Y."; and a denial sentence without a first-person subject (in English: doesn't, isn't, aren't, don't or won't, so narrative past tense stays out) followed by Instead or Rather (Stattdessen, Vielmehr) and either a reframing verb from a closed list (change, reshape, redefine, transform, reveal, ...; verändert, verwandelt, prägt, definiert, ...) or "it's about" ("geht es um"). Concrete successor actions ("Instead, we cached ...", "Instead, it returns ...", "Stattdessen cachen wir ...") stay outside the regexes. Other two-sentence forms are left to the host model, which judges them against the summary and legitimate_use. On the human reference corpus (pre-2022 texts, 260 per language) the two-sentence regexes produce no hits; the pattern as a whole triggers on 3 of 260 texts (de) and 0 of 260 (en), below the 4 % limit.

patterns.name: Appeal to familiarity
patterns.summary: A point is presented as canonical or common knowledge without evidence ("A classic.", "As we all know", "We've all been there"), borrowing the authority of a consensus that the text never shows. The imagined authority is the reader's assumed prior experience.

positive: As we all know, onboarding makes or breaks retention.
We've all been there: the deploy fails at 5 p.m. on a Friday.
The project ran over budget. A classic.
It's no secret that remote teams struggle with alignment.
negative: The novel is a classic of Russian literature and was first published in 1869.
Everyone in the office knows the door code, which is why we change it monthly.
The survey found that 62 % of respondents knew the policy.
We have all been invited to the review on Thursday.

positive: Wie wir alle wissen, entscheidet das Onboarding über die Bindung.
Jeder kennt das: Das Deployment scheitert am Freitag um 17 Uhr.
Das Projekt sprengte das Budget. Ein Klassiker.
Es ist kein Geheimnis, dass verteilte Teams mit Abstimmung kämpfen.
negative: Der Roman ist ein Klassiker der russischen Literatur und erschien 1869.
Jeder im Büro kennt den Türcode, deshalb ändern wir ihn monatlich.
Laut Umfrage kannten 62 Prozent der Befragten die Richtlinie.

patterns.legitimate_use: Shared experience is a legitimate way to connect with readers in personal essays and humor, and some facts really are common knowledge. Flag appeals that stand in for evidence on a point the reader could dispute.
patterns.fix: Replace the appeal with the evidence or example that makes the point, or state the point plainly without claiming consensus.
patterns.prevention: Do not claim that everyone knows or has experienced something. Give the evidence or the example instead.
patterns.notes: Single-source observation. The detector covers stock phrases only; claims of canonicity phrased freely ("the textbook example") need a reader's judgement. Threshold not yet calibrated against the reference corpora.

patterns.name: Assistant self-reference
patterns.summary: The chat assistant speaks about itself inside the finished text: it names itself as an AI ("As an AI language model, I can't ..."), dates its own knowledge ("As of my last knowledge update in January 2022"), states what it cannot access ("I don't have access to real-time data"), or the label of an interface button ("Regenerate response") was pasted along with the answer. The lines belong to a conversation the reader never saw and show that the output was not edited.

positive: As an AI language model, I can't add the content for you, but I can help you draft the bibliography.
As of my last knowledge update in January 2022, the hospital had not announced a new director.
I don't have access to real-time data, so please check the regulator's website for current rates.
In summary, the treatment remains contested. I'm sorry, but I am a large language model and cannot give medical advice.

The findings are summarized in Table 2.

Regenerate response
negative: As an AI researcher, I spend most of my time on evaluation, not on model training.
Since my last update in March, we have hired two engineers and closed the Berlin office.
I'm an AI ethicist by training and a product manager by trade.
The chatbot said it had no access to live prices, so I called the dealer instead.
The model's training cutoff is listed in the vendor documentation as October 2023.

patterns.legitimate_use: Articles, papers and reports about chatbots quote such lines on purpose, fiction can have an AI narrator, and a tutorial may describe the "Regenerate response" button. Flag a hit when the line speaks in the voice of the document's author and refers to the author's own nature, knowledge cutoff or access, which a human author would never claim.
patterns.fix: Delete the self-reference and everything that only makes sense in the chat (apologies, offers, limitations). If the limitation was real, replace it with the missing fact from a checked source or with a dated statement in the author's voice ("Figures as of March 2026").
patterns.prevention: Never write as the assistant inside a deliverable: no "as an AI", no knowledge-cutoff dates, no statements about what you can or cannot access. Give the content, or state plainly which fact is missing.
patterns.notes: Mechanism: the assistant's self-description leaks into a text that has a human author. Closest existing patterns: sycophant-residue (politeness formulas such as "Great question!" or "I hope this helps") and model-fingerprint-opener (stock first words such as "Certainly! Here's"). Both are conversational framing; this pattern is the assistant describing itself, its training date or its tool limits, which also occurs mid-text. reasoning-leak covers narrated deliberation, not self-identification. The Wikipedia guide lists knowledge-cutoff statements (2022 to 2023) and prompt refusals as historical indicators that have become rare in current models; Academ-AI shows they nevertheless reached hundreds of published papers. The detector requires "AI" to be followed by "language model", "assistant", "model" or "chatbot" (or punctuation after "I am an AI") so that job titles such as "an AI researcher" do not match, and leaves out the bare "since my last update", which human status updates use.

patterns.name: Belaboring the unnecessary
patterns.summary: The text defends or qualifies a minor, uncontroversial point as if answering an objection nobody raised ("I don't mean any of that as cynicism about players."). The pre-emptive defence costs space and pulls attention away from the actual argument.

detector.rubric: Find sentences that defend, justify or qualify a point that is minor or uncontroversial in context, as if pre-empting an objection that the text gives no reason to expect. Typical forms: "I don't mean this as criticism of ...", "To be clear, this is not about ...", "None of this is to say ...", "Das soll keine Kritik an ... sein", "Damit ist nicht gesagt, dass ...", when the preceding text contains nothing that a reasonable reader would take as that criticism or claim. Do not count qualifications that answer an objection the text itself raised or that a real audience is known to hold, legal or safety caveats, and corrections of a likely misreading of a technical statement. Return each pre-emptive defence as a hit.

positive: The team switched the build tool in May. I don't mean any of that as criticism of the old tool, which served us well.
We moved the stand-up to 9:30. To be clear, this is not about anyone being late; it simply fits the new time zones better.
The cafeteria now closes at three. None of this is to say that lunch is unimportant.
negative: Some readers took last week's post as an attack on the vendor. It was not: the outage was our configuration error.
This is not legal advice; consult a lawyer before you sign the lease.
The function returns null on timeout. That does not mean the request failed; it may still complete on the server.

positive: Wir haben das Build-Tool im Mai gewechselt. Das soll keine Kritik am alten Tool sein, das uns gut gedient hat.
Das Daily beginnt jetzt um 9:30 Uhr. Damit will ich niemandem Unpünktlichkeit vorwerfen; die Zeit passt einfach besser zu den Zeitzonen.
Die Kantine schließt jetzt um 15 Uhr. Damit ist nicht gesagt, dass das Mittagessen unwichtig wäre.
negative: Einige Leser verstanden den Beitrag als Angriff auf den Anbieter. Das war er nicht: Der Ausfall lag an unserer Konfiguration.
Dies ist keine Rechtsberatung; lassen Sie den Vertrag vor der Unterschrift prüfen.
Die Funktion gibt bei einem Timeout null zurück. Das heißt nicht, dass die Anfrage fehlgeschlagen ist.

patterns.legitimate_use: Writers address objections their readers actually hold, add required legal or safety caveats, and correct likely misreadings of technical statements. Flag defences against objections that nothing in the text or its audience suggests.
patterns.fix: Delete the pre-emptive defence. If a real objection exists, name it and answer it with evidence.
patterns.prevention: Do not defend points nobody disputes. Address an objection only when the reader is likely to raise it, and then answer it concretely.
patterns.notes: Single-source observation. vrid.ai describes a related mechanism ("Over-Explanation of Basics", defining obvious terms); it is kept separate because defining a term and defending against an imagined objection differ. Threshold not yet calibrated against the reference corpora.

patterns.name: Brochure tone
patterns.summary: Promotional adjectives from travel and marketing copy accumulate in expository text ("vibrant", "breathtaking", "captivating", "atemberaubend", "unvergesslich"). Each one asserts an impression where the reader needs a property they could observe or measure.

positive: Nestled between rolling hills, the vibrant town offers breathtaking views.
The new dashboard delivers a captivating experience with stunning visuals.
Our conference venue sits on a bustling, picturesque harbor that guests find unforgettable.
This hidden gem is a must-visit for every developer.
negative: The town lies 12 km north of the pass at 1,450 m and has two hotels with 80 beds in total.
Each record carries a unique identifier that the importer checks for collisions.
The captive portal redirects unauthenticated clients to the login page.
The nested loop runs in quadratic time and dominates the profile.

test_texts.text: The API answers in a breathtaking 40 ms on average.
The old harbor is vibrant in summer and quiet in winter.
The vibrant old town and the breathtaking coastline draw visitors all year.

positive: Die atemberaubende Altstadt und der bezaubernde Hafen machen jeden Besuch unvergesslich.
Unsere Software bietet ein einzigartiges Nutzererlebnis.
Das malerische Dorf liegt in einer traumhaften Bucht.
negative: Das Dorf liegt auf 1.450 m Höhe und hat zwei Hotels mit zusammen 80 Betten.
Jeder Datensatz hat eine eindeutige Kennung, die der Import auf Dubletten prüft.
Der Atemwegsinfekt dauerte bei den meisten Probanden fünf bis sieben Tage.
Die Einzelteile werden vor der Montage gezählt und gewogen.

test_texts.text: Die Schnittstelle antwortet in atemberaubenden 40 ms.
Im Sommer ist der Hafen malerisch, im Winter fast leer.

patterns.legitimate_use: Travel guides, hotel and venue marketing, product reviews and fiction use evaluative adjectives by genre; quoted customer feedback is also fine. Dismiss hits when the text is advertising copy by design and the adjective sits next to concrete details. The finding targets expository prose, technical and academic writing included, where the adjective replaces a description.
patterns.fix: Replace each adjective with an observable or measurable property: altitude, distance, opening hours, latency, a detail the reader can verify. Delete it if no such property exists.
patterns.prevention: In expository text, technical and academic writing included, do not use promotional adjectives such as "vibrant", "breathtaking", "stunning", "atemberaubend" or "einzigartig". Describe a property the reader can check instead.
patterns.notes: In technical and academic contexts a single promotional adjective already stands out, so the threshold drops to 1 hit there; all other contexts need 2. The term lists start from vibrant, breathtaking, captivating, atemberaubend, bezaubernd, einzigartig and unvergesslich and add common brochure adjectives; "captivating" also overlaps with "captivate" in hallmark-vocabulary.

patterns.name: Bullet with bold lead
patterns.summary: Lists whose items consistently start with a bold keyword and a colon, followed by a sentence that paraphrases the keyword ("**Speed:** The new engine is faster.").

positive:
- **Speed:** The new engine is faster.
- **Security:** All data is encrypted at rest.

* **Geschwindigkeit:** Die neue Engine ist schneller.
* **Sicherheit:** Alle Daten werden verschlüsselt.

- **Cost**: Lower than before.
- **Support**: Available around the clock.
negative:
- Speed: the new engine is faster.
- Security: all data is encrypted at rest.
**Speed:** The new engine is faster than the old one, according to the March benchmark.

- Install **pgvector** first.
- Then run **make test**.

- Geschwindigkeit: Die neue Engine ist schneller.
- Sicherheit: Alle Daten werden verschlüsselt.

patterns.legitimate_use: Reference material such as glossaries or API parameter lists legitimately pairs a bold term with its definition. Flag the shape when the bold lead only labels a sentence that paraphrases it and continuous prose would carry the content better.
patterns.fix: Turn the list into prose, or remove the bold and keep only items that carry distinct information.
patterns.prevention: Do not format lists as "**Keyword:** sentence". Write prose, or use plain bullets when the items are truly parallel.

patterns.name: Bullet list preference
patterns.summary: Content that a person would write as connected prose is broken into bullet or numbered lists, regardless of whether the items are parallel. The list format hides the relations between the points (cause, contrast, sequence) that prose would have to state.

positive: - Faster onboarding
1. Fill in the application form
• Schnellere Einarbeitung
2) Antrag ausfüllen
negative: Profit fell - again - in the third quarter.
3.5 million users signed up in the first week.
-5 °C is expected tonight.
Der Gewinn sank – erneut – im dritten Quartal.
3,5 Millionen Nutzer meldeten sich in der ersten Woche an.

patterns.legitimate_use: Lists suit parallel items: steps of a procedure, requirements, options, reference material. Flag lists whose items depend on each other or that a reader would understand better as a paragraph, especially in short answers.
patterns.fix: Turn the list into prose that states how the points relate (because, but, then). Keep lists for truly parallel items and procedures.
patterns.prevention: Write connected prose by default. Use a list only for parallel items, steps or reference data.
patterns.notes: Independent sources: Pangram (two pages, one cluster), arxiv-2603-27006, the Anthropic prompting documentation and an Inside Higher Ed classroom comparison. Counter-trend: some newer models produce little or no unrequested markdown (GPT-5.4 in arxiv-2603-27006; the Anthropic documentation says one newer model formats less), so the pattern may fade by model generation. Distinct from bullet-bold-lead, which concerns the bold-lead structure of list items. Threshold: 4 list items per 100 words, not yet calibrated against the reference corpora. Expected false positives in documentation and checklists.

sources.note: General preference for lists where human authors would choose prose, 9x the human baseline. Corpus size and methodology not disclosed.
"list-like structures"; bullet point lists "in the middle of the essay which rarely happens in formal human writing". Same publisher as pangram-signs-of-ai-writing, so the same independence cluster.

"bullet points enumerate where prose would suffice". With a plain essay prompt, overt markdown features (headings, bullets, bold and numbered lists counted together) reach 6.27 (GPT-4.1), 6.15 (Claude Sonnet 4) and 6.03 (GPT-4o Mini) per 1,000 words, 0 for GPT-5.4 and Llama 3.3 70B; a prose instruction removes them.
